title: Indra walks back: the dreamer isn't the self
hookLine: twice Indra finds the flaw in his teacher's answer, and twice he walks back, firewood in hand
carry: the self is not the dreamer
tomorrow: deep sleep, and the one who sees

cards: Picture the king of the gods on a road, halfway home, standing still. Indra has just spent thirty-two years with his teacher, Prajapati, and he left happy: the self, he was told, is the one you see in a pan of water.
Then, a few steps from home, the answer cracks. He has the choice every student since has had: pretend it made sense, or walk back and say, I don't understand yet.

teach.h: IF THE BODY IS BLIND, SO IS IT.
teach.b: On the road, Indra thinks it through. If the self is that reflection, then when the body is well dressed, it's well dressed. When the body is blind, it's blind.
When the body dies, it dies. I see nothing good in this.
So he turns around and walks back to Prajapati with firewood in his hands, samit-pani, the sign of a student asking to be taught. You left content, Prajapati says. Why are you back?
Indra tells him. It is so, Prajapati answers. Live here another thirty-two years.
The king of the gods signs up for thirty-two more years because one answer didn't hold. Then the next teaching: the one who moves about happily in dreams, that is the self.
Better, surely. The dreamer isn't blind when the body is blind. Indra leaves, content again.
And again, on the road, the doubt comes.
In dreams, it's as if someone is chasing him. It's as if he feels pain. He even weeps, as it were.
I see nothing good in this either. So, once more, he turns around. Here's what Hindus take from this.

teach.h: THE SELF IS NOT THE DREAMER.
teach.b: The atman, the self, isn't the body, and it isn't the dreamer either. The Upanishads count three states we pass through, waking, dream and deep sleep, and they look for the self that's there through all three.
And the way you find it is the old teacher and student way: you bring your doubt back, firewood in hand, as many times as it takes.

how: Students in many Hindu traditions return to their teacher with questions again and again; carrying firewood (samit-pani) is the traditional sign of approaching a teacher as a student.

o: the king of the gods walking back to learn more
a demon king returning to fight the gods
the king of the gods coming home to his throne

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: blind when the body is blind

s: Prajapati scolds Indra for coming back
he says: it is so. I'll explain further. live here another thirty-two years.
Indra finds the flaw on the road, before he reaches the gods
both times, halfway home, he stops and thinks it through.
the dreamer is untouched by any pain
it's not harmed by the body's faults, but in dreams it's chased and weeps.

games.q: you're Indra, halfway home. you've realized the reflection goes blind when the body goes blind. what do you do?
o: keep walking; you're the king of the gods.
turn around and go back to Prajapati with firewood in hand.
games.why: he goes back as a student, and stays another thirty-two years for the next teaching.

practice: Close your eyes and notice the pictures that start on their own, a memory, a plan, a little scene, like a dream but awake.
Don't follow them; notice that a picture is showing and something is aware of it, and when a scene pulls you in, step back to the one aware of the dream.

wordCard.voice: Indra returns. The king of the gods walks back to his teacher, twice, because the reflection and then the dreamer didn't hold up.

orig.note: Sanskrit svapna: dream, dreaming. the second answer Indra tests and finds wanting.

carryVoice: Your line: the self is not the dreamer. Tomorrow, Indra goes back a third time. See you then.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 8.10.1–4 (the dreamer; the doubt again)
